title: Growing Sure in a Sure Word
summary: Peter reminds believers of Christ’s provision, urges diligent growth in grace, and grounds hope in apostolic witness and Spirit-given prophecy.
historicalContext: Peter writes near the end of his life, aware that the death foretold by Jesus is close at hand. The letter most naturally addresses the same congregations of Asia Minor that received his earlier epistle (3:1), now facing a different danger. Persecution from outside is no longer the chief threat; teachers arising within the churches are mocking the promise of Christ’s return, treating moral restraint as optional, and dismissing the apostolic message as invented storytelling. Peter’s answer takes the shape of a final charge from a departing shepherd. He recalls what God has already given, presses believers toward steady moral growth, and appeals to two witnesses that cannot be set aside: what he himself saw and heard on the mount of transfiguration, and the prophetic Scriptures spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit. Probably written from Rome shortly before his martyrdom in the mid-sixties, the chapter carries the weight of a last testimony.
literaryContext: The chapter lays the foundation for the whole letter. After a greeting that confesses Jesus Christ as God and Saviour (1:1–2), Peter sets out the gift of divine power and promises (1:3–4) and then the believer’s answering diligence in a graded chain of virtues ending in love (1:5–11). He next states his purpose: to keep stirring his readers by reminder before he lays aside his earthly tent (1:12–15). The closing paragraph (1:16–21) supplies the ground on which the warnings of chapter 2 and the defence of Christ’s coming in chapter 3 will stand. Key words recur deliberately: knowledge, diligence, sure, remembrance, and the “power and coming” of Christ. The false prophets of 2:1 are framed against the true prophets of 1:21, and the scoffers of 3:3–4 deny precisely the coming that Peter saw foreshadowed on the holy mount.
themes: Divine power that supplies everything for godliness
Sharing God’s character through his promises
Diligent growth from faith to love

outline.title: Greeting from a Servant and Apostle
outline.summary: Peter greets those who share an equally precious faith and prays that grace and peace may increase through knowing God and Jesus.

outline.title: Divine Power and Precious Promises
outline.summary: Christ’s power has supplied all that life and godliness require, and his promises enable believers to share the divine character while fleeing corruption.

outline.title: Diligent Growth and Sure Calling
outline.summary: Believers answer God’s gift by adding grace to grace, proving their calling and receiving a rich entrance into Christ’s eternal kingdom.

outline.title: A Reminder Before Departure
outline.summary: Knowing his death is near, Peter resolves to keep his readers mindful of the truth after he is gone.

outline.title: Witnesses of Majesty and the Sure Word
outline.summary: Apostolic eyewitness of the transfiguration and Spirit-borne prophecy together confirm the power and coming of Jesus Christ.

verses.bibleText: Simon Peter, a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ, to them that have obtained like precious faith with us through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter opens with the apostle’s full Hebrew name. Many early manuscripts read “Simeon” instead of the usual “Simon,” the form James used of him at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:14). Beside it stands “Peter,” the rock-name Jesus gave him. The old fisherman and the commissioned apostle are one man, and both names belong to the one who now writes his final pastoral charge.

He calls himself first “a servant,” a bondservant owned by his Master, and then “an apostle,” one sent with his Lord’s authority. The two titles do not compete. Peter’s right to speak rests entirely on belonging to Jesus Christ and being sent by him. That matters in a letter written against teachers who claimed freedom from authority and offered their own clever ideas (2:1, 19). Peter brings no private wisdom of his own; he comes as a servant carrying a commission.

The readers “have obtained like precious faith with us.” The verb suggests receiving something by allotment, the way an inheritance is assigned. Faith is a gift apportioned by God, not a prize won by superior insight. “Like precious” means equally valuable, of the same honour. Believers who never walked with Jesus in Galilee hold a faith that stands on equal footing with the apostles’ own. No inner circle possesses a superior salvation. The false teachers would soon imply that they had access to something higher; Peter insists that ordinary believers already share the full treasure.

This faith comes “through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ.” The Greek joins “God” and “Saviour” under a single article, the same pattern Peter uses for “Lord and Saviour” in 1:11, 2:20, and 3:18. The most natural sense is “our God and Saviour, Jesus Christ.” Peter, who once confessed Jesus as “the Son of the living God,” here names him plainly as God. His righteousness is both his fairness in granting the same faith to all and the saving righteousness by which he puts sinners right with himself.

wordNotes.term: ἰσότιμον (isotimon) — like precious
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective describes something of equal honour, value, or standing. It was used of people granted the same rights or privileges as others. Peter applies it to the faith his readers received: it carries the same worth as the faith of the apostles who were eyewitnesses. The word levels every claim to spiritual rank within the church.

wordNotes.term: τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος (tou theou hēmōn kai sōtēros) — God and our Saviour
wordNotes.explanation: One article governs both nouns, so the phrase most naturally names a single person: Jesus Christ is both God and Saviour. The identical construction appears in Titus 2:13, and Peter repeats the pattern with “Lord and Saviour” later in this letter. The opening line therefore makes a clear confession of Christ’s deity.

verses.bibleText: Grace and peace be multiplied unto you through the knowledge of God, and of Jesus our Lord,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Grace and peace” was the standard Christian greeting, and Peter used the same words with the same verb in his first letter (1 Peter 1:2). The readers already possess grace and peace. What Peter prays for is increase: “be multiplied.” Grace is God’s unearned favour and the strength it brings; peace is the settled wholeness of a life reconciled to God. Both are meant to grow, and the letter ends on the same note with the command to “grow in grace” (3:18).

The channel of that growth is “the knowledge of God, and of Jesus our Lord.” Here, unlike verse 1, the grammar distinguishes two persons: the Father and the Son. Peter uses a strengthened word for knowledge, one that implies personal acquaintance and recognition, not information collected at a distance. It is the knowledge that begins at conversion, when a person comes to know God through Christ, and that deepens as the relationship matures. This word will return in verses 3 and 8 and in 2:20, marking it as a theme of the letter.

The emphasis is pointed. The false teachers would offer novel ideas and a so-called liberty (2:19). Peter answers that grace and peace multiply as believers come to know the Father and his Son more truly; speculation adds nothing to them. Such knowledge changes the knower. It is relational, moral, and lasting, and it is the soil from which everything else in this chapter grows.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιγνώσει (epignōsei) — knowledge
wordNotes.explanation: Peter prefers this fuller form over the simpler word for knowledge when speaking of knowing God and Christ. In context it describes the personal acknowledgment and relationship that begin when someone comes to faith and continue to deepen. It is the kind of knowing that shapes conduct, which is why Peter can tie it to grace, peace, godliness, and fruitfulness.

verses.bibleText: According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now explains how grace and peace can increase. The opening phrase, “According as,” introduces the ground: Christ’s “divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness.” The power most naturally belongs to Jesus, the last person named in verse 2 and the one called God in verse 1. The verb is a word for bestowing a gift, and its tense presents the gift as already given and still in force. Nothing essential has been withheld.

“Life and godliness” cover the whole range of what a believer needs. Life includes the new spiritual life that begins in Christ, and godliness is the reverent, practical devotion to God that shows itself in daily conduct. Peter does not say that believers already display every grace; the following verses call for strenuous growth. He says the resources are already supplied. No believer can plead that God has left him without what is required to live faithfully.

These gifts come “through the knowledge of him that hath called us.” The caller may be the Father, who is usually described as calling in the New Testament, or Christ, who called fishermen from their nets. The difference is small, since Father and Son act together. The call is “to glory and virtue,” or as many manuscripts read, “by his own glory and virtue.” On that reading, people are drawn by what they see of Christ himself: the radiance of his divine majesty and the moral excellence of his character. Peter had watched both firsthand, in miracles, in the cross, and on the mount.

The verse confronts any religion of self-improvement. Godliness does not begin with human resolve. It begins when Christ’s character attracts a person and his power equips that person to follow. The effort Peter will demand in verse 5 is a response to what has already been given, never a substitute for it.

wordNotes.term: εὐσέβειαν (eusebeian) — godliness
wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes reverent devotion to God expressed in fitting conduct. It joins inward piety to outward behaviour, describing a life ordered by respect for God. Peter uses it four times in this short letter, setting it against the irreverence of the false teachers. Here it names one of the purposes for which Christ’s power has supplied every needed resource.

wordNotes.term: ἀρετῇ (aretē) — virtue
wordNotes.explanation: In ordinary Greek the term meant excellence of any kind and, in moral contexts, outstanding goodness. Applied to God it describes the excellence of his character and his praiseworthy acts. Peter first uses it of Christ, who calls by his own excellence, and then in verse 5 urges believers to supply the same quality in their own lives.

verses.bibleText: Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Whereby” points back to Christ’s glory and excellence. Through them “are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises.” The word Peter chooses for promises appears only here and in 3:13, where it names the promise of new heavens and a new earth. That connection suggests that the promises include everything God has pledged in salvation, with special focus on the coming of Christ and the restored creation. The promises are precious because they cost Christ so much; they are exceedingly great because their fulfilment surpasses anything human beings could ask.

The purpose of the promises is stated plainly: “that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature.” Peter borrows language his Greek-speaking readers would recognise from philosophical talk about what humans share with the gods, but he fills it with biblical meaning. He does not teach that human beings become God or absorb the divine essence. Elsewhere Scripture describes the same reality as being renewed in the image of the Creator, being changed into Christ’s likeness from glory to glory, and sharing God’s holiness. Humanity was made in God’s image; sin marred that image; Christ came to restore it. To partake of the divine nature is to have God’s moral character reproduced in a human life by the power of the Spirit, a work begun at the new birth and completed when Christ appears.

The second half of the verse states the other side of that renewal: “having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.” The verb pictures flight, an active escape from danger. The corruption in view is moral decay rooted in disordered desire. Peter will use similar vocabulary in 2:18–20 for those who once escaped and then returned to the mire. Sharing God’s nature and fleeing the world’s corruption are two aspects of one movement. A believer is not saved in sin but from it.

This verse lifts the Christian life far above respectable behaviour. The goal is likeness to God himself, and the means are his own promises, taken hold of by faith. Every promise believed becomes a point at which God’s character begins to take shape in a person.

wordNotes.term: θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως (theias koinōnoi physeōs) — partakers of the divine nature
wordNotes.explanation: Koinōnoi are sharers or partners in something held in common. Peter speaks of sharing in God’s nature in the sense of his moral qualities: holiness, goodness, and incorruptible life as God gives it. The context of fleeing corruption and adding virtues shows that he means transformation of character, not a change of humans into deity. It is the restoration of the image of God that sin had defaced.

wordNotes.term: ἀποφυγόντες τῆς … φθορᾶς (apophygontes tēs … phthoras) — having escaped the corruption
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes escaping by flight, as one would run from a burning house. Phthora means decay or ruin and here refers to the moral rot of a world driven by selfish desire. Peter repeats the verb in 2:18 and 2:20, where he warns of people who fled this corruption and then turned back into it.

verses.bibleText: And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And beside this” is better rendered “for this very reason.” Because Christ has supplied everything for life and godliness, and because his promises open the way to share God’s character, believers must now bring every effort to bear. Divine provision does not make human diligence unnecessary; it makes diligence reasonable and fruitful. God’s gift comes first, and the believer’s earnest cooperation follows from it.

“Giving all diligence” pictures bringing in alongside, contributing one’s full energy beside what God has already given. Peter will use the word for diligence again in verses 10 and 15 and in 3:14. A lazy or careless Christianity is foreign to his thinking.

The verb translated “add” carried a vivid background. It was used of a wealthy citizen who paid for a public chorus or festival and supplied it generously at his own expense. Peter’s point is lavish provision: believers are to furnish their faith richly with the qualities that belong to it. The list that follows is sometimes called a ladder, though it works more like a chain in which each grace is supplied “in” the one before and gives it fuller expression.

The chain begins with “faith.” Faith is the foundation on which every other quality rests, the trusting reception of God’s gift in Christ, and so it stands first instead of appearing as one more item on the list. To it believers add “virtue,” the moral excellence Peter has just attributed to Christ himself (v. 3). Then comes “knowledge,” here the ordinary word for knowing, which in this context means practical moral discernment, the wisdom to see what God’s will requires in specific situations. Faith without excellence becomes barren profession; excellence without discernment can become zeal without direction. Peter wants the whole person furnished.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιχορηγήσατε (epichorēgēsate) — add
wordNotes.explanation: The verb comes from the world of civic generosity, where a benefactor bore the cost of equipping a chorus or public celebration. In the New Testament it means to supply or furnish abundantly. Peter calls believers to furnish their faith richly with virtue and the graces that follow, and in verse 11 he uses the same verb for God richly supplying an entrance into the kingdom.

wordNotes.term: σπουδὴν πᾶσαν (spoudēn pasan) — all diligence
wordNotes.explanation: Spoudē means eagerness, earnest effort, or zeal that makes haste to accomplish its goal. With “all” it describes wholehearted exertion. Peter places this human diligence directly after describing God’s complete provision, showing that grace awakens effort instead of excusing passivity.

verses.bibleText: And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chain continues with three linked qualities. To knowledge believers add “temperance,” self-control. Moral discernment is of little use unless a person can actually govern desire. Self-control was prized in the Greek world, but Peter places it in a new setting: it is a fruit of the Spirit and a fitting answer to the “corruption … through lust” described in verse 4. The false teachers of chapter 2 will be marked by exactly the opposite, unrestrained appetite. Knowledge that does not discipline the appetites becomes the kind of knowledge those teachers boasted of while living in excess.

To self-control is added “patience,” the steady endurance that keeps going under pressure. Here the pressure in view is not chiefly persecution but the ongoing pull of temptation and the discouragement of a long wait. Self-control wins a single battle; endurance keeps winning when the struggle continues day after day. Christian endurance rests on hope in God and in the promised coming of Christ, which chapter 3 will defend.

To endurance is added “godliness,” the reverent devotion to God already named in verse 3. Its placement here guards against a self-made morality. Self-control and endurance can be practised with pride, as though the believer were his own achievement. Godliness keeps every discipline turned toward God, humble and grateful, recognising that the strength for each step comes from him. A person may grit his teeth through temptation; godliness turns that endurance into worship.

wordNotes.term: ἐγκράτειαν (enkrateian) — temperance
wordNotes.explanation: The word means mastery over oneself, especially over bodily appetites and passions. Paul lists it among the fruit of the Spirit and preached it before Felix alongside righteousness and judgment. In 2 Peter it stands in deliberate contrast to the self-indulgence of the false teachers, who promised liberty while being slaves of corruption.

wordNotes.term: ὑπομονήν (hypomonēn) — patience
wordNotes.explanation: Hypomonē is endurance that remains steady under a heavy load. It is active perseverance, not passive resignation. In this chain it follows self-control, describing faithfulness sustained over time against continuing temptation and the strain of waiting for Christ’s promised return.

verses.bibleText: And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chain reaches its climax in two forms of love. To godliness believers add “brotherly kindness,” the warm affection that binds members of God’s family. In ordinary Greek usage the word described love among blood siblings, but in the New Testament it extends to all who share the faith. Devotion to God that does not issue in tender care for fellow believers is incomplete. Peter had urged the same affection in his first letter, calling his readers to love one another fervently with a pure heart (1 Peter 1:22).

The placement is significant. Self-control, endurance, and reverence could produce an austere, inward-looking piety. Brotherly kindness turns that piety outward. In a congregation threatened by teachers who exploited people for gain (2:3, 14), sincere family affection would be a mark of authentic faith and a protection against division.

The final step is “charity,” love in its fullest sense. This is the self-giving love that seeks another’s good at personal cost, the love God shows in giving his Son. It reaches beyond the household of faith to neighbours and even enemies. Peter does not end with knowledge, as the false teachers might have wished, or with ecstatic experience, but with love. Every earlier quality finds its completion here.

The list moves from faith to love, the same pairing that frames so much of the New Testament’s teaching on the Christian life. Faith receives God’s gift; love expresses God’s character. Between them lie the virtues by which that character is formed. Read as a whole, the passage is not a scheme for rising to God by effort. It is a portrait of what Christ’s divine power produces in a life that takes hold of his promises and keeps cooperating with his grace.

wordNotes.term: φιλαδελφίαν (philadelphian) — brotherly kindness
wordNotes.explanation: The word combines affection with the idea of siblings. Outside the Bible it usually described love within a natural family. Christians applied it to the church as God’s household, so it names the warmth, loyalty, and practical care that believers owe one another.

wordNotes.term: ἀγάπην (agapēn) — charity
wordNotes.explanation: Agapē is the love that wills and works for the good of another, even at great cost to oneself. It is the love by which God loved the world and the love Christ commanded his disciples to show. Placing it last, Peter makes it the crown and goal of the whole sequence of graces.

verses.bibleText: For if these things be in you, and abound, they make you that ye shall neither be barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now gives the reason for such diligence. “If these things be in you, and abound” describes more than a minimal presence. The qualities just listed are to belong to the believer and to keep increasing. Growth in grace is a continuing direction of life, never a stage completed and left behind.

Where these graces grow, they keep a person from being “barren” and “unfruitful.” The first word means idle or ineffective, like a worker standing unused in the marketplace. The second pictures a tree or field that yields no harvest. A Christian rich in faith, self-control, kindness, and love cannot remain idle; such graces press outward into service and produce results. The false teachers, by contrast, will be called wells without water and empty clouds (2:17), all appearance and no yield.

The sphere of this fruitfulness is “the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Peter returns to the fuller word for knowledge used in verses 2 and 3. The virtues are not an independent moral programme. They grow out of knowing Christ and lead into knowing him better. Fruit that is cut off from him withers; fruit that springs from union with him has no fixed limit. Jesus said the same thing when he spoke of branches abiding in the vine.

wordNotes.term: ἀργοὺς οὐδὲ ἀκάρπους (argous oude akarpous) — barren nor unfruitful
wordNotes.explanation: Argos describes something idle, inactive, or useless; it is used of workers standing about with nothing to do. Akarpos means without fruit. Together they describe a profession of faith that yields nothing. Peter states the matter negatively, but the implied promise is positive: growing graces make a believer active and fruitful.

verses.bibleText: But he that lacketh these things is blind, and cannot see afar off, and hath forgotten that he was purged from his old sins.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The opposite condition is now described. The person who “lacketh these things” is a professing believer who has stopped growing; Peter is not describing a pagan who never heard the gospel. Such a person “is blind, and cannot see afar off.” The second phrase translates a single verb from which the English word “myopic” comes. It may describe squinting, the half-closed eyes of someone whose sight is failing. Spiritual neglect does not usually produce instant blindness. It narrows the field of vision until only what is near at hand, the concerns and pleasures of the present world, remains in focus. Eternal realities, including the coming of Christ, fade from view.

The root of the problem is forgetfulness: he “hath forgotten that he was purged from his old sins.” The cleansing refers to the forgiveness received when the person first came to Christ, publicly marked in baptism. Peter does not say the cleansing never happened, nor that one lapse cancels it. He says it has been forgotten. When a believer loses sight of how much was forgiven, gratitude cools, the motive for holiness weakens, and growth stalls. Forgetting forgiveness and failing to grow belong together.

The warning is sharpened by what follows in chapter 2, where Peter describes those who escaped the world’s pollution through knowing Christ and were entangled again. Spiritual myopia is the early stage of that tragedy. The remedy is simple, though not easy: remember the cleansing, and let that memory set the heart moving forward again. Peter himself had once denied his Lord and been restored; he knew how powerfully remembered mercy can renew a life.

wordNotes.term: μυωπάζων (myōpazōn) — cannot see afar off
wordNotes.explanation: This rare verb describes nearsightedness or the squinting of failing eyes. Peter uses it to portray spiritual vision narrowed to the immediate and the earthly, unable to keep eternal realities in view. It gives English the word “myopic.”

wordNotes.term: λήθην λαβών τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ (lēthēn labōn tou katharismou) — hath forgotten that he was purged
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “having taken forgetfulness of the cleansing.” Katharismos refers to purification from sin, the cleansing God grants at conversion and seals in baptism. Peter’s concern is that such cleansing can be neglected in memory, robbing the believer of the gratitude that fuels growth.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore the rather” draws a conclusion from verses 3–9. Since God has supplied so much, and since neglect leads to blindness, believers should be all the more eager. Peter addresses them warmly as “brethren,” the only time he uses that address in the letter, and repeats the call to diligence from verse 5.

They are to “make your calling and election sure.” Calling is God’s gracious summons through the gospel; election is his choice of a people for himself in Christ. Both are God’s acts. Peter does not imply that believers create their own election. The word “sure” was used in legal and commercial settings for a guarantee or a confirmed title. Believers confirm their calling by living in a way that corresponds to it, adding the graces of verses 5–7. Election in Scripture is never an arbitrary decree that renders human response meaningless. God’s choice is made in Christ, according to his foreknowledge, and it calls for a faith that perseveres. The grace of God can be received in vain, and Peter wants his readers to make certain that is not their story.

The promise attached is strong: “if ye do these things, ye shall never fall.” The verb means to stumble. Peter does not claim that growing Christians will never sin; James uses the same word to say that “in many things we offend all.” The point is that they will not stumble in such a way as to fall away from God’s call into ruin. Steady growth is the safeguard against the apostasy described in chapter 2.

This verse holds together assurance and responsibility. Believers need not live in anxious uncertainty, because God’s call is real and his provision is complete. Yet assurance is not a static possession detached from life. It is strengthened as faith keeps moving toward love. Certainty about God’s calling grows as a believer keeps walking in the path that call has opened, more than by searching inwardly for a feeling.

wordNotes.term: βεβαίαν … τὴν κλῆσιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν (bebaian … tēn klēsin kai eklogēn) — calling and election sure
wordNotes.explanation: Bebaios means firm, reliable, or legally guaranteed. Klēsis is God’s call through the gospel; eklogē is his choosing of a people in Christ. Peter asks believers to confirm these divine acts by a corresponding life, so that what God has offered and begun is made steadfast in their experience.

wordNotes.term: οὐ μὴ πταίσητέ (ou mē ptaisēte) — ye shall never fall
wordNotes.explanation: The double negative expresses strong certainty. Ptaiō means to stumble or trip, and in moral contexts to fail. Here it refers to a fall that would forfeit God’s call, not to every lapse. The promise belongs to those who keep adding grace to grace.

verses.bibleText: For so an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For so” means “in this way,” by growing in grace and confirming the calling. The result is that “an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom.” Peter uses the same verb as in verse 5. Believers are to furnish their faith with virtue; God will furnish them with a rich entrance into his kingdom. The human supply is answered by a divine supply far greater.

“Abundantly” means richly or generously. Peter pictures a welcome in full measure, far removed from someone barely slipping through a closing gate. Peter does not suggest that virtue purchases admission; the kingdom remains a gift. Yet the generosity of the welcome corresponds to a life that has kept faith with the One who called.

The kingdom is “everlasting,” the only place in the New Testament where that adjective is joined directly to the word kingdom. It belongs to “our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ,” a title that echoes verse 1. Though believers already live under Christ’s rule, the entrance here lies in the future, at the day when he comes in power and glory. Peter will defend that hope at length in chapter 3, describing new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells. The whole chain of graces leads home.

wordNotes.term: πλουσίως ἐπιχορηγηθήσεται … ἡ εἴσοδος (plousiōs epichorēgēthēsetai … hē eisodos) — an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly
wordNotes.explanation: Eisodos is a way in or an entering. The passive verb indicates that God is the one who supplies it, and plousiōs, “richly,” describes the generosity of his welcome. The repeated verb from verse 5 forms a deliberate echo between the believer’s diligent supply and God’s abundant reward.

wordNotes.term: αἰώνιον βασιλείαν (aiōnion basileian) — everlasting kingdom
wordNotes.explanation: Aiōnios describes what belongs to the coming age and lasts without end. Linked with the kingdom of Christ, it points to the reign that Daniel foresaw would never be destroyed and that will be fully established at the Second Coming.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance of these things, though ye know them, and be established in the present truth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With “Wherefore” Peter turns from exhortation to his purpose in writing. Because so much hangs on growing in grace, and because the entrance into the kingdom is at stake, he will “not be negligent to put you always in remembrance of these things.” The phrase may also be read as “I will always be ready” or “I intend always” to remind them. Either way, reminder is his chosen ministry for the time that remains.

He acknowledges that they already “know them” and are “established in the present truth.” This is not flattery. Faithful teaching often consists less in telling people something new than in keeping familiar truth alive in their minds. Danger rarely comes from total ignorance; it comes from truths known so long that they no longer govern the heart. Peter’s readers were about to hear teachers offering novelties. His safeguard is repetition of the gospel they had received.

“Established” echoes the charge Jesus gave Peter on the night of the betrayal: “when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.” The same root lies behind both words. The apostle who once wavered is now steadying others, still fulfilling his Lord’s commission at the close of his life.

“The present truth” means the truth that is present with them, the body of apostolic teaching they had been given. It is the shared deposit of the faith, held in common by the whole church. At the same time the phrase reminds every generation that God’s unchanging truth must be grasped and held in the particular circumstances where his people live, especially when error presses upon them.

wordNotes.term: ἐστηριγμένους (estērigmenous) — established
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to set firmly, to fix, or to strengthen so that something stands without wavering. Jesus used it when he told Peter to strengthen his brethren after his own restoration. The perfect participle describes a settled condition already achieved, which Peter wants preserved against the unsettling influence of false teachers.

wordNotes.term: τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθείᾳ (tē parousē alētheia) — the present truth
wordNotes.explanation: The participle means “being present” or “at hand.” The phrase describes the truth that has come to the readers and is now with them, the apostolic gospel they received. Paul uses the same verb of the gospel that “is come unto you.” It stresses that this truth is their present possession, to be kept and lived in their own day.

verses.bibleText: Yea, I think it meet, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by putting you in remembrance;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter considers it “meet,” right and fitting, to keep stirring his readers “as long as I am in this tabernacle.” The tabernacle, or tent, is his mortal body. The image fits a pilgrim people. A tent is a temporary dwelling, easily taken down, suited to travellers who have not yet reached home. Peter knows his present life is short and provisional.

He does not use the image to teach that a person is a soul living inside a disposable shell. Paul uses the same picture and makes clear that the Christian’s longing is not to be unclothed but to be clothed with the immortal body God gives at the resurrection. Peter’s hope, likewise, looks to the coming of Christ and the eternal kingdom, not to an escape of the soul at death.

While he lives, Peter intends “to stir you up by putting you in remembrance.” The verb means to rouse thoroughly, like waking a sleeper. Believers who drift into spiritual drowsiness need to be woken. A faithful shepherd does not leave them in comfortable sleep while wolves are approaching.

wordNotes.term: σκηνώματι (skēnōmati) — tabernacle
wordNotes.explanation: The word means a tent or temporary dwelling. Used of the human body, it highlights frailty and impermanence. It recalls Israel’s tent-dwelling in the wilderness and the pilgrim life of the patriarchs. In biblical usage the hope beyond this tent is a resurrection body, not a disembodied existence.

wordNotes.term: διεγείρειν (diegeirein) — to stir you up
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to wake fully or to rouse. The Gospels use it of the disciples waking Jesus in the storm. Peter applies it to his ministry of reminder: he wants to rouse the minds of believers so that they stay alert to truth and danger.

verses.bibleText: Knowing that shortly I must put off this my tabernacle, even as our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter’s urgency rests on knowledge: “shortly I must put off this my tabernacle.” The word “shortly” can mean soon or suddenly. Either sense fits. He was an old man, and the death Jesus had foretold for him was a violent one. Mixing his metaphors naturally, he speaks of putting off his tent as one would lay aside a garment.

The source of his certainty is “even as our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me.” The clearest occasion is the conversation by the Sea of Galilee after the resurrection, when Jesus told Peter that in old age another would bind him and carry him where he did not wish to go, signifying “by what death he should glorify God.” Peter had lived for decades with that word. Whether the Lord gave him a fresh indication as the time drew near, or whether he simply recognised that the old prophecy was now ripening, he speaks with calm conviction.

The tone is striking. There is no panic and no bitterness. A man who once fled from danger and denied his Master now faces execution with composure, and his chief concern is the welfare of the flock. The same Lord who predicted his death had also restored him and commissioned him to feed the sheep. That commission shapes his final days.

Peter’s acceptance of death also matters for the argument of the letter. He does not expect to be alive at Christ’s return. The scoffers of chapter 3 would mock the delay of the promise, but Peter’s confidence in the coming of Christ does not depend on seeing it in his own lifetime.

wordNotes.term: ταχινή … ἡ ἀπόθεσις (tachinē … hē apothesis) — shortly I must put off
wordNotes.explanation: Apothesis means a laying aside or removal, a term more commonly used of clothing than of tents. Tachinos can mean coming soon or coming swiftly. Peter speaks of his death as an imminent laying aside of his mortal body, an event Jesus had foretold.

verses.bibleText: Moreover I will endeavour that ye may be able after my decease to have these things always in remembrance.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter will “endeavour,” using the verb of diligence that has run through the chapter (vv. 5, 10). He applies to himself the same earnestness he urges on his readers. His aim is that “after my decease” they may “be able … to have these things always in remembrance.” His ministry of reminder is meant to outlast him.

The word for “decease” is exodos, departure. Luke uses it in the transfiguration account, where Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about the exodus he would accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter was present on that occasion, and it can hardly be accidental that the next verse turns to the transfiguration. The word also recalls Israel’s exodus from Egypt, a departure that led toward an inheritance.

How will his readers remember after he is gone? The most direct answer is this letter itself, a written reminder they could reread whenever the need arose. The words “always” or “at any time” suggest a resource available for every occasion. Some early Christians also connected Peter’s preaching with the Gospel of Mark, which preserved his testimony about Jesus. Either way, Peter recognises that the church will need a permanent record of apostolic witness once the apostles are gone. That concern anticipates the role of the written New Testament: the foundation laid by eyewitnesses remains available to every generation in Scripture.

wordNotes.term: ἔξοδον (exodon) — decease
wordNotes.explanation: Exodos means a going out or departure, and it was used as a gentle way of speaking about death. Its use in Luke’s transfiguration account for Christ’s death at Jerusalem links Peter’s own departure with the scene he is about to describe. The word frames death as a departure under God’s direction.

verses.bibleText: For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now defends the foundation of everything he has said. “For we have not followed cunningly devised fables” answers a charge that was evidently being made. The false teachers dismissed the apostolic message about Christ’s return as myth, a clever story invented to frighten people into moral restraint. The word Peter uses gives English the term “myths,” and in the ancient world it often described tales about gods appearing among humans that educated people regarded as fiction. Peter rejects the label outright. The gospel was not crafted by skilful storytellers.

What the apostles “made known” was “the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The two nouns form a single idea: his coming in power. The word for coming, parousia, was used of a royal visit, the arrival of a king or emperor to a city with all the ceremony that attended it. In the New Testament it regularly describes the Second Advent, and Peter will use it again for the promise the scoffers deny (3:4) and the day believers await (3:12). The concern of this paragraph is therefore the future return of Christ in glory, a literal and visible event of which the transfiguration was a preview.

The apostles’ proof is that they “were eyewitnesses of his majesty.” Peter, James, and John had seen with their own eyes the glory of Christ on the mount. They did not repeat secondhand legends or construct theories. They testified to what they had seen. In the ancient world eyewitness testimony carried the greatest weight in any court, and Peter brings it forward deliberately.

The word for eyewitnesses was sometimes used of those admitted to the highest level of a religious initiation, where secret sights were revealed. If Peter intends any echo, the contrast is sharp. What he saw was not a ritual secret for a privileged few but a public revelation of Christ’s glory meant to be proclaimed to all.

The apostolic faith is rooted in history. Christianity does not rest on inspiring ideas detached from events. It rests on what God did in Jesus Christ, seen and heard by reliable witnesses, and on what he has promised to do when Christ comes again.

wordNotes.term: σεσοφισμένοις μύθοις (sesophismenois mythois) — cunningly devised fables
wordNotes.explanation: Mythos referred to stories, often legends about the gods, regarded as untrue. The participle describes something cleverly contrived or sophisticated in a deceptive way. Peter denies that the apostolic preaching of Christ’s coming was an artful fiction. Paul likewise warned against fables that turn people from the truth.

wordNotes.term: δύναμιν καὶ παρουσίαν (dynamin kai parousian) — power and coming
wordNotes.explanation: Parousia means presence or arrival and was used of a ruler’s official visit. In the New Testament it is the regular term for Christ’s return in glory. Joined with power, it describes his coming as a mighty, visible event, the same coming Jesus described as the Son of man arriving in the clouds with power and great glory.

verses.bibleText: For he received from God the Father honour and glory, when there came such a voice to him from the excellent glory, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now describes what the eyewitnesses saw and heard. Christ “received from God the Father honour and glory.” Honour lay in the Father’s public declaration about his Son; glory was the radiance that shone from Jesus as his face blazed like the sun and his clothing became white as light. On the mount the veil of his humanity was drawn back for a moment, and the disciples glimpsed the majesty that belongs to him and that will be seen by all when he returns.

The voice came “from the excellent glory.” This expression is a reverent way of naming God himself. The Gospels tell of a bright cloud overshadowing them, recalling the cloud of God’s presence that filled the tabernacle and the temple. Out of that cloud the Father spoke.

The words were, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” They echo the Father’s declaration at the baptism of Jesus and draw on two great passages of the Old Testament. Psalm 2 speaks of the King whom God calls his Son and to whom he gives the nations as an inheritance. Isaiah 42 speaks of the chosen Servant in whom God delights. The voice thus identifies Jesus as both the royal Son who will rule and the Servant who suffers. Peter’s wording differs slightly from the Gospel accounts, as one would expect from a man recalling an experience he had told many times.

The point for Peter’s argument is clear. God himself has declared Jesus to be his Son and has invested him with glory. The coming in power that the apostles preach is the open display of the same honour the Father conferred on the mount. Those who deny it set themselves against the voice of God.

wordNotes.term: τῆς μεγαλοπρεποῦς δόξης (tēs megaloprepous doxēs) — the excellent glory
wordNotes.explanation: Megaloprepēs means magnificent, majestic, befitting greatness. The phrase is a reverent way of referring to God, using his glory to stand for his presence. It corresponds to the bright cloud of the transfiguration accounts, the visible sign of God’s presence familiar from Israel’s history.

wordNotes.term: ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός (ho huios mou ho agapētos) — my beloved Son
wordNotes.explanation: “Beloved” can carry the sense of “only” or “uniquely dear,” as in the description of Isaac. The declaration marks Jesus as the unique Son who shares the Father’s love and authority, and it echoes the words spoken from heaven at his baptism.

verses.bibleText: And this voice which came from heaven we heard, when we were with him in the holy mount.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter adds the testimony of hearing to the testimony of sight. “This voice which came from heaven we heard.” The pronoun “we” is emphatic. Peter speaks for the three disciples Jesus took with him: Peter, James, and John. They were not reporting a rumour; they were present. Under the law of Moses a matter was established by two or three witnesses, and on the mount there were three.

The phrase “when we were with him” underlines that presence. The apostles had walked with Jesus, shared his journeys, and stood beside him when the glory broke through. Their authority rested on that companionship.

Peter calls the place “the holy mount.” The mountain itself is not named in the Gospels, and its location remains uncertain. Its holiness came from the revelation that took place there. As the ground before the burning bush became holy because God was present, so this mountain was sanctified by the glory of Christ and the voice of the Father. The phrase may also recall the holy hill of Zion in Psalm 2, where God sets his King, tying the transfiguration to the enthronement of the Son that Peter expects to be fully revealed at his coming.

wordNotes.term: ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ ἁγίῳ (en tō orei tō hagiō) — in the holy mount
wordNotes.explanation: Old Testament writers often spoke of God’s holy mountain, especially Zion. Peter applies the phrase to the mount of transfiguration, holy because God revealed his glory and spoke there. The language links the event with God’s self-revelation on Sinai and with the enthronement of his King.

verses.bibleText: We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now brings forward a second witness. “We have also a more sure word of prophecy.” The comparative has been read in different ways. Some take it to mean that Scripture is more reliable than the apostles’ experience, but Peter is hardly downgrading the voice of God he has just described. Others take “more sure” as simply “very sure.” The most natural reading in context is that the prophetic word has been made more sure, confirmed, by what the apostles witnessed. The Old Testament prophets foretold a Messiah who would suffer and then reign in glory. On the mount the apostles saw that glory anticipated, and their experience confirmed what the prophets had written. Prophecy and eyewitness testimony stand together, each strengthening the other.

“The word of prophecy” refers to the whole prophetic witness of the Old Testament, which looks forward to the coming of God’s kingdom and of the Son of man in glory. The apostles constantly reasoned from these Scriptures, showing that Jesus fulfilled them. Prophecies fulfilled in history give confidence that the prophecies yet unfulfilled will come to pass in their time.

Believers “do well” to “take heed” to this word “as unto a light that shineth in a dark place.” The light is a lamp, and the dark place is murky, squalid, gloomy. Peter’s picture is of a traveller making his way at night through a dismal, dirty place with only a small lamp to guide each step. That is the world as Peter sees it, darkened by sin and confused by false teaching. The prophetic word does not remove the darkness, but it shows the way through it.

The lamp is needed “until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts.” The day is the day of the Lord, the coming of Christ that ends the night of this age. The day star is the morning star, the light-bringer that heralds sunrise. Scripture calls Christ himself “the bright and morning star.” When he comes, the lamp will no longer be needed, because the full light of his presence will fill the world. The phrase “in your hearts” indicates that his appearing will bring complete inward illumination to his people. Even now, as believers take heed to the prophetic word, a foretaste of that dawn begins to shine within them, keeping hope alive while they wait.

wordNotes.term: βεβαιότερον τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον (bebaioteron ton prophētikon logon) — a more sure word of prophecy
wordNotes.explanation: Bebaios means firm or confirmed, the same root used for making one’s calling sure in verse 10. The comparative form most naturally means the prophetic word stands even firmer, having been confirmed by the events the apostles witnessed. The phrase describes the prophetic Scriptures as a whole, which pointed forward to Christ’s glory.

wordNotes.term: φωσφόρος (phōsphoros) — day star
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “light-bearer,” the word was used of the morning star, the planet seen just before sunrise. It heralds the coming day. Applied here to Christ, it points to his return, which ends the night of this present age and brings the full light of God’s kingdom.

verses.bibleText: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Knowing this first” introduces a principle of the highest importance for anyone who takes heed to the prophetic word. Peter states it negatively: “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.” The phrase “of the scripture” makes clear that he is speaking of the written prophecies contained in the Old Testament.

The words “private interpretation” have been understood in two main ways. One reading takes them to refer to the reader: no individual may interpret prophecy according to his own fancy. The other reading takes them to refer to the prophet: no prophecy arose from the prophet’s own interpretation of things. The next verse begins with “for” and explains that prophecy did not come by human will but from God through the Spirit. That explanation fits the second reading best. Peter’s chief point concerns the origin of prophecy. The prophets were not offering their personal explanation of events or their own speculations about the future. They spoke messages that originated with God.

This was a pointed answer to the false teachers. If the prophets were merely giving human opinions, their predictions of Christ’s coming and of judgment could be dismissed. Peter insists they cannot. What the prophets said, God said.

The principle also carries a clear implication for interpretation. Since prophecy comes from God, its meaning is not ours to invent. Readers must seek the sense the Spirit intended, comparing Scripture with Scripture and submitting their own ideas to the text. Peter will later warn of people who twist the Scriptures to their own destruction (3:16). The cure for private distortion is to let the Word explain itself under the guidance of the same Spirit who gave it. Peter does not place Scripture under a human authority that alone may read it. Every believer may read the prophetic word, and every believer must read it humbly, as a message from God to be received, not a mirror for personal opinion.

wordNotes.term: ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως (idias epilyseōs) — private interpretation
wordNotes.explanation: Epilysis means an explanation or solving, used of interpreting a riddle, a dream, or a parable. Idios means one’s own. In context Peter most likely means that no prophecy arose from the prophet’s own explanation of things; its source was God. The verbal form describes Jesus explaining his parables privately to his disciples.

wordNotes.term: τοῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες (touto prōton ginōskontes) — knowing this first
wordNotes.explanation: “First” here means “above all” or “as a matter of primary importance,” not the first item in a sequence. Peter uses the same expression in 3:3 to introduce the coming of scoffers. It marks a foundational principle that must govern how prophecy is received.

verses.bibleText: For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter explains why no prophecy of Scripture is of private origin: “For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man.” Prophecy never originated with human initiative. A prophet could not decide to prophesy and then produce a message by his own effort or desire. The initiative belonged entirely to God, who chose what to reveal, when to reveal it, and through whom. The false prophets of chapter 2 are precisely those who speak out of their own minds.

Instead, “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.” Many manuscripts read “men spoke from God,” which emphasises the divine source of their words. Either reading carries the same essential meaning. The prophets were real human beings who spoke in their own languages and styles, yet what they spoke came from God.

The key word is “moved,” the verb meaning to bear or carry. Peter used the same verb in verses 17 and 18 for the voice that was borne from heaven. Luke uses it in Acts 27 of a ship driven along by the wind when the sailors could no longer steer. The picture is vivid. The prophets were carried along by the Holy Spirit as a sailing vessel is carried by the wind. The wind supplies the power and determines the direction, while the ship is fully involved in the voyage. The Spirit did not erase the personalities of the prophets, but he so directed them that their words were God’s message.

This verse, together with Paul’s teaching that all Scripture is God-breathed, forms one of the central statements of the Bible’s own view of its origin. Scripture is both fully human and fully from God. Its authority rests on the Spirit who moved its writers, whatever their gifts as authors. For Peter’s readers, that settled the matter. The prophecies of Christ’s coming in glory were not human speculation. They were God’s word, and they would be fulfilled as surely as the prophecies of his first coming had been.

wordNotes.term: ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενοι (hypo pneumatos hagiou pheromenoi) — moved by the Holy Ghost
wordNotes.explanation: Pherō means to carry or bear along. The passive participle describes the prophets being borne along by the Holy Spirit, much as a ship is carried by the wind. The image highlights the Spirit as the driving power behind prophecy while the prophets remained active speakers. Peter uses the same verb for the voice borne from heaven at the transfiguration.

wordNotes.term: θελήματι ἀνθρώπου (thelēmati anthrōpou) — by the will of man
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase sets human desire or initiative against divine origin. Scripture often contrasts what comes from human will with what comes from God. Here Peter denies that any prophecy began with a human decision. Ezekiel condemned prophets who followed their own spirit and had seen nothing.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: If God has already given everything needed for godliness, why does Peter still call for such strenuous effort?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Christ’s divine power and promises make a godly life possible, and believers answer that gift with diligent growth, held steady by the apostolic witness and the Spirit-given word of prophecy until the day of his coming.
discussionQuestions: How does Peter keep God’s gift (vv. 3–4) and human diligence (vv. 5–7) together without making salvation a reward for effort?
Why does the list of virtues begin with faith and end with love?
What does spiritual shortsightedness look like, and how does forgetting forgiveness cause it?
Why would the transfiguration be such strong evidence for the Second Coming?
What does verse 21 teach about how Scripture came to be, and how should that shape the way we read it?
commonMisunderstandings: Sharing the divine nature does not mean becoming God; it describes moral renewal into God’s likeness.
Making election sure does not mean earning election; it means confirming God’s gracious call through a faithful life.
“No private interpretation” is first a statement about where prophecy came from, not a license for church authorities alone to read Scripture.
Peter’s tabernacle language does not teach that a conscious soul departs at death; his hope rests on Christ’s coming and the resurrection.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep grace and growth in one movement: God gives all things through knowing Christ, and that gift sets believers to work, steadied by a word that did not originate with human will.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Take hold of the promises Christ has given, add grace to grace with steady diligence, and keep the lamp of God’s word burning until the morning of his appearing.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Jesus Christ, our God and Saviour, gives cleansing from sin and power for a new life, and the Scriptures that announce his return were given by the Holy Spirit.
flow: The world is marked by corruption that springs from disordered desire.
Christ purges past sins and, by his divine power, supplies all that a godly life requires.
His promises renew people in God’s likeness as they flee corruption and grow in grace.
The apostles saw his majesty, and Spirit-given prophecy confirms that he will come again.
Those who receive his call are invited to make it sure and enter his eternal kingdom.
simpleIllustrations: A lamp in a dark room does not remove the night, but it lets a person walk safely until morning comes.
A sailing ship moves because the wind fills its sails; the prophets spoke because the Spirit carried them.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you receive the cleansing Christ offers and let his promises begin to reshape your life as you wait for his appearing?
cautions: Do not present the chain of virtues as a ladder by which a person climbs into God’s favour.
Do not suggest that a believer who struggles has lost forgiveness; Peter warns against forgetting it.
Do not set the transfiguration and Scripture against each other; Peter uses them together.

reflectionQuestions: Which of God’s promises do I most need to take hold of in order to flee a particular corruption?
Where in my life has faith stalled instead of growing into self-control, endurance, and love?
Have I forgotten how much I have been forgiven, and how has that dulled my spiritual sight?
What truths do I already know that I need to be reminded of again this week?
How much attention am I actually giving to the prophetic word as a lamp for dark days?
